title: A Dynamic General Equilibrium Theory of Purpose-Bound Money
subtitle: Household Security, Labor Supply, Endogenous Capacity, Innovation, and Long-Run Welfare
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic general-equilibrium research program for purpose-bound money (PoC), an enforceable and restricted purchasing entitlement that may be exercised only against eligible goods or services and that generates separately funded reimbursement obligations to suppliers. It asks whether reliable access rights can transform not merely current consumption but the long-run organization of labor, human capital, production, innovation, and public finance. A heterogeneous-household model nests cash consumption, purpose-restricted expenditure, incomplete asset markets, endogenous labor, health and skill formation, firms’ pricing and investment, differentiated-product entry, and a fiscally constrained issuer. The formal analysis distinguishes restricted purchasing power from a conventional per-unit subsidy, nonconvertibility from solvency, a real supply response from a price transfer, and equilibrium private utility from ethically relevant capabilities. We derive conditional fixed-price dominance of cash, comparative-static price incidence, resourceaccounting identities, capital-investment threshold results, conditions for locally stable policy dynamics, and a welfare decomposition that explicitly includes those who do not receive the entitlement. A synthetic two-type, two-sector numerical economy supplies an exactly reproducible within-period general equilibrium and a transparent transition under specified investment and health-adjustment rules. Its counterexamples reveal that targeting, financing, and generalequilibrium income effects can lower aggregate output or unweighted welfare even when recipients gain. The numerical transition is intentionally not represented as a calibrated HANK solution; fully forward-looking heterogeneous-agent dynamics are stated as an extension with explicit equilibrium conditions and computational requirements. The analysis identifies the circumstances under which PoC could create additional real provision and enlarge practical freedom, and the empirical evidence needed to distinguish it from cash transfers, ordinary vouchers, and direct capacity procurement.

title: Access Over Output
subtitle: A Supply-Constrained Monetary Framework for World Development Without Prior Industrialization
abstract: This paper proposes a fundamental reorientation of development economics: in the contemporary global economy, the binding constraint on welfare for the world's poorest populations is not the absence of productive capacity but the absence of institutional mechanisms through which latent demand can be expressed as effective purchasing power. Advanced economies persistently operate below full capacity while billions lack access to goods already being produced—a structural paradox that production-centered frameworks cannot adequately address. To resolve this, the paper introduces a Supply-Constrained Monetary Framework operationalized through Trade-PoC (trade-linked, purpose-bound currency), an instrument whose issuance is anchored to verified estimates of effective global supply. By conditioning demand creation on available supply, the framework achieves price stability by institutional design rather than ex post price adjustment, without requiring prior domestic industrialization in recipient economies. Convertibility of Trade-PoC revenues is governed by the γᵢ mechanism—a performance-based function spanning eight dimensions including output expansion, institutional quality, and supply diversification—that aligns firm behavior with the system's objectives and induces endogenous capacity expansion. Formal proofs establish equilibrium existence, uniqueness, and stability. Proof-of-concept support is drawn from WFP electronic voucher programs across four countries. The paper further specifies the governance architecture of a new global coordinating institution and a three-phase implementation strategy. The framework does not replace the developmentalist tradition but expands the development policy solution space to include access design alongside productive transformation.

title: An Analysis of Demand and Supply under Purpose-Bound Money
subtitle: Consumer Welfare, Producer Incentives, and the Dynamics of Market Equilibrium
abstract: This paper develops a demand-and-supply framework for purpose-bound money, defined as a capped purchasing entitlement tied to eligible transactions and credible supplier settlement. The analysis distinguishes a household balance from a per-unit subsidy and connects individual balance exhaustion to aggregate demand, prices, actual redemption, producer surplus, and money-metric welfare. Restricted purchasing power can replace existing cash expenditure, expand eligible consumption, or remain unused. The corresponding supply response depends on capacity, market power, entry costs, settlement credibility, and the horizon over which firms can invest. A dynamic investment model identifies the present value of capacity rents required for expansion; complementary models analyze receivable pledgeability, risk sharing, product variety, quality incentives, congestion, and common-input scarcity. Fiscal and physical constraints are treated jointly, with explicit accounting for correlated redemption risk and the cost of guarantees. Exact synthetic experiments show that recipients and suppliers can both gain while net social welfare declines, and calculate the external-benefit thresholds required to reverse that ranking. Comparisons with equal-cost cash, conventional vouchers, and capacity procurement identify the additional market friction that a purpose-bound contract must resolve to justify its restrictions. The paper supplies conditional propositions, derivations, counterexamples, and reproducible calculations; it does not estimate empirical treatment effects or claim that programmability creates real resources. Its central research question is when enforceable targeted demand can be converted into reliable new provision rather than higher prices, redistribution of scarce access, or unfunded claims.
keywords: purpose-bound money; restricted transfers; consumer welfare; supplier investment; market design; settlement risk; endogenous supply; fiscal incidence.

title: Beyond Universal Basic Income: Can Purpose-Bound Transfers Deliver More Welfare with Less Inflation?
subtitle: Monetary Financing, Endogenous Supply, and Social Welfare
abstract: Universal basic income (UBI) and purpose-bound money (PoC) are often compared as alternative instruments for redistributing purchasing power. That comparison is incomplete without examining financing, settlement, behavioral responses, endogenous supply, and the consolidated balance sheet of the state. This paper develops a fiscal–monetary framework in which unconditional transfers and purpose-restricted transfers can be financed either by taxes, public debt, or money creation; recipients optimize across eligible and ineligible goods; suppliers endogenously adjust capacity, quality, and prices; and central-bank liabilities change composition as restricted claims are redeemed. The central analytical result is conditional rather than categorical. Restricted transfers may generate more targeted consumption and lower sectoral inflation than unrestricted cash when procurement, competition, and elastic supply jointly offset the additional demand concentration. Without credible supply expansion, however, earmarking can intensify rather than alleviate sector-specific inflation. Furthermore, denomination in noninterest-bearing digital claims does not by itself avoid interest-bearing reserve liabilities after redemption; expiration reduces only outstanding claims that have genuinely lapsed, while taxoffset redemption may substitute foregone public revenue for monetary liabilities. We examine these propositions alongside randomized evidence from cash and voucher programs in Ecuador, Mexico, Kenya, Malawi, and the United States, and construct an independent descriptive series from U.S. SNAP fiscal data for 1990–2025. A transparent structural sensitivity exercise exhibits an explicit supply-response threshold at which PoC’s target-sector price effect becomes smaller than that of cash, together with conditional reserve-remuneration trajectories. The evidence Beyond Universal Basic Income · 1 establishes neither unconditional superiority of PoC nor the equivalence of restricted digital claims to conventional in-kind transfers. Instead, it identifies testable design conditions under which the coupling of purchasing power with verifiable supply commitments may improve welfare per unit of consolidated fiscal–monetary cost.
keywords: purpose-bound money; basic income; earmarked transfers; central-bank balance sheet; reserve remuneration; endogenous supply; cash transfers; vouchers; monetary financing; social welfare; market design.

title: Designing an AI-Enabled Global Central Bank
subtitle: Dual-Layer Monetary Protocols, Sovereign Autonomy, and Computational Coordination
abstract: This paper develops a theory of a Global Central Bank (GCB) that coordinates purpose-bound service finance through common international protocols and autonomous national policy. The proposed institution combines shared rules for issuance, verification, settlement, and interoperability with national control of eligibility, welfare priorities, and funding. Artificial intelligence enters as a costly information technology for demand estimation, supply assessment, dynamic issuance planning, matching, anomaly detection, and policy simulation. Its contribution is conditional: learning can make large-scale, timely, heterogeneous coordination economically feasible when it reduces decision and interaction costs sufficiently, but conventional methods remain the appropriate benchmark. The framework separates consumer entitlements, provider receivables, real capacity, and payment resources. Twelve propositions across explicitly delimited submodels characterize institutional subsidiarity, funded issuance, participation, information value, pathwise commitment coverage, robust control, a scale threshold for AI adoption, decentralized convex allocation, and feedback stability. A deterministic funding invariant can preserve coverage despite arbitrary forecasting errors under stated accounting and execution assumptions; it does not guarantee service quality or useful targeting. A trained synthetic experiment compares fixed rules, linear and quadratic regression, and gradient boosting under identical budgets and capacities. Flexible learning lowers allocation loss in a stable nonlinear environment but performs worse after a specified structural break. Federated estimation, privacy, strategic reporting, human review capacity, model concentration, and sovereign consent are treated as economic constraints. The paper proposes a modular empirical agenda that separately identifies the effects of interoperability and AI. The case for a separate GCB depends on measurable gains over national programs and treaty networks, rather than on a claim of costless issuance, universal participation, or unconditional algorithmic superiority.
keywords: global central bank; purpose-bound money; fiscal federalism; sovereign participation; institutional design; artificial intelligence; matching; coalition formation; monetary settlement; computational economics; public-private platforms.

title: Designing Money
subtitle: Purpose-Bound Currency and the End of Macroeconomic Constraints
abstract: This paper develops a new monetary framework in which allocation is embedded directly into the structure of money. In standard macroeconomic models, money is assumed to be fungible, and policy operates by adjusting aggregate conditions through interest rates, fiscal transfers, or regulation. This architecture generates well-known constraints, including cross-sector spillovers, financial amplification, and the limits of monetary autonomy in open economies. We propose an alternative system based on purpose-bound currency (PoC), a class of nonfungible monetary instruments restricted to specific domains of use. By construction, PoC eliminates cross-domain substitutability and embeds allocation at the point of issuance. We show that this seemingly simple modification has far-reaching implications for equilibrium structure. First, in a general equilibrium framework, PoC induces segmentation: consumption, prices, and liquidity become domain-specific, and cross-sector spillovers are structurally eliminated. Second, in both discrete-time DSGE and continuous-time stochastic control models, we demonstrate that financial amplification mechanisms and global financial cycle transmission do not propagate into PoC-governed domains. Third, in a mechanism design setting, we show that incentive compatibility is achieved by construction, as misallocation becomes infeasible rather than merely suboptimal. These results imply that several canonical constraints in macroeconomics—including aspects of the monetary trilemma—are not fundamental, but arise from the use of a single, fungible monetary instrument. When monetary functions are separated across domain-specific currencies, these constraints are relaxed at the structural level. The paper provides a unified theoretical framework—combining general equilibrium, dynamic macroeconomics, and mechanism design—to show that monetary architecture itself can serve as a policy instrument.

title: Embassies of Welfare
subtitle: Transnational Public Service Delivery, Institutional Architecture, and Fiscal Sovereignty
abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical and institutional framework for what we term Embassies of Welfare (EoWs)—semi-sovereign, publicly mandated entities established by advanced welfare states to deliver public services directly within the territorial boundaries of host countries. Departing from the traditional Westphalian assumption that welfare provision is an exclusively domestic function of the nation-state, we argue that a fundamental reconfiguration of fiscal sovereignty is both analytically warranted and institutionally feasible in a world characterized by deep economic interdependence, cross-border risk propagation, and persistent gaps in public-service delivery across jurisdictions. We proceed in five stages. First, we demonstrate that existing mechanisms for cross-border welfare provision—development aid, multilateral lending, and humanitarian transfers—are structurally deficient: they are episodic rather than standing, conditional rather than rights-based, and intermediated rather than direct. Second, we articulate the normative foundations of EoWs, grounding them in Rawlsian principles of global justice, Sen's capability approach, and the economics of public goods with transboundary externalities. Third, we analyze the institutional architecture of EoWs, including their governance structures, funding mechanisms, legal status, and relationship to hostcountry sovereignty. Fourth, we develop a formal model of EoW equilibrium, demonstrating conditions under which welfare-exporting states and recipient populations are jointly better off, and characterizing the optimal allocation of EoW services across competing locations. Fifth, we situate EoWs within the broader purpose-oriented fiscal architecture proposed in the parent paper, showing how they interact with Purpose-Oriented Currencies, Purpose-Bound Accounts, and Capital-at-Birth mechanisms to form an integrated system of transnational welfare. We conclude that Embassies of Welfare represent not merely a marginal innovation in development policy, but a qualitative transformation in how advanced economies can exercise global leadership— through demonstrated competence in service delivery rather than through financial transfers, diplomatic pressure, or military projection. The institutional implications are profound: welfare, like trade and capital, must be reconceptualized as a globally mobile asset, capable of flowing toward populations in need regardless of their citizenship or geographic location.

title: Empirical Foundations of a Purpose-Bound Economy
subtitle: Evidence on Household Demand, Program Scale, Market Adjustment, and Long-Run Development
abstract: This paper develops a disciplined empirical foundation for a broader research program in purposebound finance, universal meal rights, human-capital access, supplier contracting, market competition, and international welfare coordination. The proposed purpose-bound monetary architecture has not been implemented at the proposed global scale. Consequently, this paper neither estimates the causal effect of that architecture nor represents simulations as observed evidence. Instead, it separates the mechanisms on which the architecture relies and studies them with five independently verifiable bodies of observed data, combined with a narrowly interpreted review of existing randomized evidence. The original empirical exercises comprise: food expenditure and income for 235 historical Belgian households; an international panel of 142 countries observed at five-year intervals between 1952 and 2007; 203 quarters of United States macroeconomic data from 1959Q1 through 2009Q3; United States Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program national administrative totals for fiscal years 2000–2025; and a selected 24country cross-section of OECD public social expenditure for 2024. The observational estimates are computed from archived real datasets with heteroskedasticity-robust, country-clustered, or heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent uncertainty estimates as appropriate. Household food expenditure is increasing but less than proportional to income; however, the historical Engel sample contains no transfer experiment. The conditional income–longevity association remains positive in a two-way fixed-effects panel but changes substantially under population weighting and regional restrictions. Investment growth in historical US data is several times more volatile than consumption growth, but contemporaneous output–investment regressions do not identify a demand-induced investment effect. The SNAP administrative series documents a large, sustained, financed restricted-transfer program but does not identify its general-equilibrium supply consequences. A separate review of published experiments distinguishes directly established treatment effects from analogy. The results support a modular empirical research agenda, not a verdict that a global purpose-bound monetary system is welfare-improving. The paper specifies a source-to-claim audit, formal identification boundaries, sensitivity tests, equilibrium accounting restrictions, and a falsifiable design for future multi-market trials. A separate analytical extension derives conditional thresholds for price adjustment, credible supplier investment, and incremental welfare superiority relative to equal-cost cash support with identical capacity procurement. Its numerical cases are disclosed hypothetical scenarios, not estimated treatment effects.
keywords: purpose-bound finance; restricted transfers; Engel curves; social protection; market design; heterogeneous households; panel data; dynamic general equilibrium; program evaluation; welfare; public finance; external validity.

title: Ending Hunger Through Market Design
subtitle: The Economics of Universal Meal Rights
abstract: Hunger persists despite unprecedented levels of global food production. In many modern economies, food insecurity is increasingly a problem of access rather than supply. Millions of individuals struggle to secure reliable meals, while restaurants and other food-service providers frequently operate below capacity. This coexistence of unmet nutritional needs and underutilized productive resources suggests a structural market coordination failure. This paper introduces Universal Meal Rights (UMR) and proposes Universal Meal Insurance (UMI) as a new institutional framework for guaranteeing access to ordinary daily meals. Unlike conventional welfare programs based on means-testing, UMI treats meal access as a universal social right. The system is implemented through Meal-Specific Purpose-Oriented Currency (Meal-PoC), a non-transferable, non-accumulable, and automatically expiring monetary instrument redeemable exclusively for ordinary meals. The paper further develops a model of capacity-constrained monetary issuance, in which Meal- PoC creation is linked to the productive capacity of restaurants, cafeterias, and food supply networks. By connecting purchasing power directly to available meal-producing capacity, the framework seeks to expand access while limiting inflationary pressures. More broadly, the paper reframes meals as a form of economic infrastructure rather than a welfare benefit. By combining universal rights, purpose-oriented currency, market-based delivery, and capacity-constrained issuance, it proposes a new market-design approach to food security capable of reducing hunger, improving affordability, and strengthening local food economies in an age of abundance.

title: From Coercion to Design
subtitle: Labor Markets, Subsistence, and the Transition Problem
abstract: This paper reexamines labor supply and welfare through the lens of subsistence constraints and develops a theory of economic transitions when such constraints are removed. In standard models, labor supply is treated as a continuous choice governed by marginal trade-offs. We show that this framework breaks down once baseline consumption is guaranteed: labor supply becomes a participation problem characterized by a threshold condition, and the observed equilibrium reflects a distorted outcome sustained by implicit coercion. Specifically, when subsistence binds, the equilibrium wage lies below the true reservation wage, generating a gap that is not priced in market outcomes. Eliminating subsistence constraints does not lead to a smooth adjustment to a new equilibrium. Instead, it creates a discontinuity: participation collapses if compensation remains below the reservation threshold. We formalize this as a transition problem and show that standard policy responses—such as full internalization or static subsidies—either induce collapse or generate persistent distortions. We propose a state-contingent, self-extinguishing policy rule that bridges this gap. The rule ensures participation by guaranteeing that effective compensation meets the reservation threshold, while preserving incentives for wage adjustment and technological change. We prove that the resulting dynamics are monotone and convergent: wages and productivity increase, the gap shrinks, and subsidies vanish endogenously. The mechanism is robust to heterogeneity, multi-sector environments, and automation, and can be embedded in a DSGE framework with non-convex labor supply. The main contribution of the paper is to shift the focus of economic analysis from equilibrium selection to path design. Labor markets are not neutral outcomes of preferences and technology but are shaped by institutional constraints. Once these constraints change, equilibrium becomes a function of the transition path. This paper provides a framework for designing such paths, transforming labor supply from a coercion-based equilibrium into a system governed by explicit design.

title: From Credentials to Competence
subtitle: Redesigning Professional Education: Modular Learning, University Certification, and Labor Market Matching
abstract: Professional employment is often allocated through educational pipelines in which access to advanced instruction, assessment, social networks, and employer recognition is bundled with admission to a degree program. This bundling offers benefits—coherent curricula, peer effects, intensive supervision, and credible accreditation—but it also creates an economically consequential exclusion margin. A worker who does not enter a selective university may be unable to obtain externally credible proof of skill even when she can acquire the relevant knowledge. The expansion of massive open online courses and micro-credentials has not eliminated this problem, because access to content is not equivalent to progression through foundational prerequisites, trustworthy evaluation, or recognition by employers. This paper develops a federated Global University Skills Network (GUSN) that separates selected instructional and assessment functions from degree admission while preserving academic autonomy and the distinctive purposes of full degrees. Participating universities offer sequenced, non-degree modules with common competency metadata; independent or jointly governed examinations verify achievement; employers participate in task specification and supervised work samples; and public authorities may finance access and completion support without guaranteeing jobs or substituting for regulated licenses. The analysis integrates a multidimensional human-capital production function, a Bayesian model of employer screening, a sequential learner decision problem, a two-sided adoption equilibrium, an assignment model with finite vacancies, and a planner’s problem with equity, fiscal, and quality constraints. It derives conditions under which modular provision expands feasible occupational choice, improves posterior precision, stimulates training supply, and yields welfare improvements—and equally specifies circumstances in which credential inflation, displaced hires, fixed educational bottlenecks, or market power defeat those gains. Empirically, the manuscript distinguishes published causal evidence from illustrative Monte Carlo experiments and develops a multi-arm randomized evaluation, employer audit, staggered-adoption design, data dictionary, cost-effectiveness framework, and preregistration protocol. The principal claim is conditional rather than utopian: university-grade professional learning can be widened substantially without universal degree admission, but employment effects require independently verified competence, practical experience, employer recognition, and sufficient demand for trained labor.

title: From Fragility to Design
subtitle: Eliminating Bank Run Equilibria through Purpose-Oriented Money
abstract: This paper proposes a purpose-oriented monetary architecture that eliminates financial fragility at its structural source. In standard frameworks, such as the Diamond–Dybvig Model, bank runs arise from fixed liquidity constraints, demandable claims, and sequential service, generating strategic complementarities and multiple equilibria. Existing policy responses— most notably the lender-of-last-resort framework emphasized by Ben Bernanke—stabilize such systems ex post but leave their underlying fragility intact. The framework developed here departs from this paradigm by redesigning the monetary system itself. It introduces endogenous liquidity issuance tied to real supply capacity, replaces demandable deposits with purpose-contingent monetary claims, and removes sequential service. These changes eliminate first-mover advantages and collapse strategic complementarities, yielding a unique equilibrium in which run dynamics cannot arise. This result is formalized in a continuum-agent model, establishing that run equilibria are not supported under the proposed architecture. Embedding the system in a dynamic general equilibrium environment shows that financial shocks no longer propagate through credit constraints, thereby weakening the link between financial instability and real economic fluctuations. The model further incorporates a Capital-at-Birth (CaB) mechanism, which improves access to investment opportunities, reduces inequality, and increases steady-state output. Key implementation challenges are also addressed. A dynamic mechanism design framework demonstrates that efficient allocation can be approximately implemented under asymmetric information, with informational frictions generating bounded inefficiencies rather than systemic instability. A dual-system transition path ensures that the shift from balance-sheetbased finance to purpose-oriented liquidity can be achieved without liquidity contractions or coordination failures. Private financial institutions continue to play a central role in information production, even as liquidity provision is centralized. Taken together, the analysis suggests a shift in perspective: financial instability need not be managed through continuous intervention, but can be eliminated through institutional design. The proposed architecture replaces equilibrium multiplicity with uniqueness, transforming crises from an inherent feature of financial systems into a preventable outcome of their structure.

title: From Redistribution to Design
subtitle: Capital at Birth and the Global Investment System
abstract: This paper proposes a structural alternative to redistribution by redefining the initial conditions of economic participation. In standard frameworks, inequality is treated as an outcome to be corrected through taxation and transfers, leaving the distribution of capital at entry unchanged. We argue that this approach is inherently limited. We introduce a system of Capital at Birth (CaB), in which all individuals receive an equal allocation of investment-bound capital at birth. This capital is non-consumable and is managed within a globally coordinated investment architecture. Rather than distributing income, the system generates and allocates returns through a purpose-bound consumption framework, separating capital accumulation from consumption. The proposed Global Investment System combines centralized issuance with decentralized asset management, leveraging existing financial institutions to allocate capital efficiently at scale. By decoupling capital allocation from national fiscal capacity, the system avoids sovereign debt constraints and enables universal participation. We show that this framework transforms the foundations of economic distribution, shifting from ex-post redistribution to ex-ante design. It preserves incentives for labor, supports longterm capital accumulation, and reduces structural inequality by equalizing initial capital endowments. The model also generates distinct implications for growth, labor supply, and financial stability. More broadly, the paper demonstrates that inequality can be addressed not only through redistribution, but through the design of economic systems that shape outcomes at their origin.

title: From Triffin to a Global Reserve Currency
subtitle: Joint-Backing Elastic Liquidity and the Design of a Global Reserve Bank
abstract: International reserve demand is global, while the institutions supporting reserve assets remain predominantly national. This paper develops a Global Reserve Bank issuing settlement balances and reserve securities denominated in an International Dollar. The proposal preserves national currencies and separates international reserve services from domestic monetary stabilization. Its contribution is a contractual framework linking reserve demand, asset pooling, currency-specific liquidity, limited sovereign support, and voluntary participation. A replication benchmark establishes that relabeling existing payoffs adds no opportunity under frictionless access. A pooling result identifies when enforceable transfers expand statewise support capacity without creating aggregate wealth. A reservechoice model derives instrument demand from payment shortfalls, and a constrained issuance problem equates marginal service value with operating, liquidity, and support costs. The analysis distinguishes denomination from backing, liquidity loans from capital, and nominal guarantees from credible contributions. A reproducible numerical illustration using artificial inputs shows that common support can expand feasible issuance while optimal issuance remains below that boundary. Operating costs can reverse the welfare ranking, and an equivalent lower-cost decentralized network can dominate a common issuer. The institutional case is therefore conditional on enforceability, additional service value, and participation. The paper offers a specified alternative for organizing international monetary commitments rather than an empirical estimate of its benefits or a claim that a new currency eliminates national fiscal constraints.
keywords: international monetary system; reserve assets; Triffin dilemma; sovereign commitment; liquidity insurance; institutional design.

title: Fungibility, Not Quantity
subtitle: A New Theory of Money and Inflation
abstract: Does monetary expansion necessarily generate inflation? Standard monetary theory—ranging from the Quantity Theory to modern DSGE models—implicitly assumes that money is fully fungible across uses. This paper develops a general theory of purpose-constrained currency (PoC), in which money is non-fungible and restricted to specific domains of expenditure. Under non-fungibility, the canonical relation 𝑀𝑉= 𝑃𝑌 becomes structurally misspecified. Money is instead represented as a vector of domain-specific balances, and inflation emerges as a local phenomenon rather than an aggregate outcome. Monetary expansion is shown to be inflation-neutral under well-defined conditions: demand saturation, slack capacity, and issuance aligned with domain-specific supply. Cross-domain inflation spillovers vanish, while provider competition can generate deflationary reallocation effects. A dynamic formulation characterizes the optimal issuance policy via a Hamilton–Jacobi– Bellman framework, yielding a state-dependent rule with full issuance in slack states and throttling under binding constraints. The results are robust to partial fungibility, stochastic shocks, and heterogeneous agents. A mechanism design framework establishes incentive compatibility and eliminates lobbying distortions through rule-based classification. Nonfungibility is shown to be implementable as a cryptographically enforceable constraint using zero-knowledge proofs, with negligible leakage across domains. Quantitative simulations calibrated to sectoral data produce near-zero inflation under targeted issuance and generate substantial welfare gains relative to fungible transfers. The findings imply a reinterpretation of monetary theory: money is not a scalar, but a vector over purposes, and inflation depends on the structure of money rather than its aggregate quantity.

title: Global Sovereign Debt Resets and Fiscal Resilience
subtitle: Coordinated Creditor Redemption, Contingent Fiscal Reserves, and Inflation-Constrained Recovery
abstract: This paper evaluates a treaty-based, exceptional international sovereign debt reset in which eligible creditor claims are redeemed in their lawful currencies and public issuance rights are separated from issued conventional monetary liabilities and genuinely funded national fiscal reserves. The program is considered only when routine debt-management tools, including verified productivity-linked purpose-bound fiscal substitution, are insufficient under a transparent social-welfare and debt-distress test. It is not a claim that recorded government bonds can be extinguished without creating other obligations or real resource costs. The revised architecture explicitly separates three mutually compatible, but institutionally independent, instruments: ordinary productivity-backed purpose-bound money (PoC) used to replace verifiable fiscal spending and retire bonds gradually; a sectoral PoC conversion rule used to manage PoC-related temporary price pressure without breaching provider contracts; and a distinct extraordinary conventional-monetary redemption window used in a sovereign crisis. The article develops stock-flow accounting that prohibits counting an already retired security twice, preserves creditor contractual claims, and differentiates equal nominal issuance rights from unequal safe execution rates. It incorporates bond collateral scarcity, currency mismatch, cashdemand inflation, investor expectations, real-income distribution, provider settlement liabilities, reserve-fund withdrawal limits, and dynamic trigger incentives. A transitory increase in inflation is not mechanically treated as failure when medium-term household real purchasing power and production improve, but durable inflation or eroded essential access can rule out issuance. Official fiscal and debt evidence remains descriptive, while all reset-specific numerical simulations are transparently hypothetical. The result is a falsifiable conditional framework, not a demonstrated gain from universal periodic debt monetization.
keywords: Sovereign debt; monetary financing; asset swaps; seigniorage; fiscal dominance; international monetary coordination; sovereign wealth funds; transitory inflation; real purchasing power; mechanism design; dynamic optimal stopping. Global Sovereign Debt Resets and Fiscal Resilience | 1

title: Globalizing Scientific Opportunity
subtitle: A Consortium-Based Architecture for Universities, Innovation, and Economic Development
abstract: The international distribution of scientific capability is neither a neutral consequence of comparative advantage nor an immutable constraint on development. Research universities, laboratories, doctoral training, venture finance, and firms are connected through cumulative processes that may amplify initial advantages and leave late-industrializing economies dependent on imported technologies. This paper proposes a Global University and Innovation Consortium (GUIC): a treaty-enabled, academically autonomous network in which leading research universities and locally governed institutions jointly establish teaching and research centers across developing regions. Faculty from participating universities rotate through multi-year programs while permanent local appointments supply continuity; governance is shared, research agendas are codesigned, and intellectual-property rules protect the capacity of host institutions to accumulate and commercialize knowledge. A financing architecture combines sovereign contributions, philanthropic and development-bank funding, and narrowly scoped purpose-bound education and research instruments. The paper distinguishes a purpose-bound claim on verified local capacity from real foreign-exchange resources necessary to purchase imported laboratories, equipment, and visiting faculty services. A multi-region model links learning, research productivity, human-capital retention, firm entry, export capabilities, and external balances. It characterizes complementarities, threshold effects, potential welfare gains, and failure conditions, including academic dependency, fiscal dominance, inflation, migration, and geopolitical capture. An empirical program integrates university-program administrative records, matched firm outcomes, geocoded innovation data, staggered adoption designs, randomized oversubscription, synthetic controls, and openscience audits. Existing evidence from the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence, Carnegie Mellon University Africa, and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology establishes feasibility of elements rather than causal proof of the new architecture. Explicitly illustrative simulations explore policy sensitivity without being represented as observed treatment effects. The central proposition is not that all economies should manufacture the same products or achieve perpetual trade surpluses; it is that global institutions can widen the set of locations capable of producing, adapting, and commercializing advanced knowledge, thereby expanding productive opportunity and long-run welfare.
keywords: research universities; knowledge diffusion; development economics; international consortia; human capital; innovation systems; technology transfer; purpose-bound money; institutional design; industrial transformation; empirical identification.

title: Invisible Welfare
subtitle: Protecting Dignity through Privacy-Preserving, Predictive, and Scalable Social Protection
abstract: Welfare institutions often require people to reveal their poverty in order to obtain relief from it. This paper develops a privacy-preserving, predictive, and scalable alternative that identifies legally eligible needs, minimizes repeated disclosure, and delivers support through ordinary transactions without marking recipients to merchants or bystanders. The proposal shares Banerjee and Duflo’s normative commitment to dignity, agency, and the lived circumstances of the poor, while distinguishing intensive human-centered learning and care from the routine delivery technology appropriate for millions. A formal model combines heterogeneous take-up, stigma, disclosure risk, targeting error, choice, supply responses, and economies of scale. It derives conditions favoring invisible automatic provision and conditions favoring personintensive or universal alternatives. Verified findings are separated from a transparent synthetic simulation. The empirical agenda specifies factorial trials, quasi-experimental rollouts, market spillover analysis, and independent privacy audits. Rather than assuming that algorithmic prediction is benign, the paper treats wrongful exclusion, digital disadvantage, surveillance, and loss of agency as binding constraints. The contribution is a testable institutional framework, not a claim that automation has already been shown to outperform existing social protection.

title: Land, Power, and Access
subtitle: Renewable Energy Exports, Artificial-Intelligence Infrastructure, and Development without Prior Industrialization
abstract: This paper develops and quantitatively disciplines a development strategy in which African countries monetize land-intensive renewable electricity and geographically mobile artificial-intelligence (AI) computation to acquire foreign exchange and expand household access to internationally traded goods and services. The proposal is motivated by a distinction between the capacity to produce a broad domestic manufacturing basket and the institutional ability to command goods already produced somewhere in the world. Building on Lee (2026), Access Over Output, we specify an energy-to-access mechanism linking renewable endowments, foreign offtake contracts, host-country ownership, export receipts, and a rules-based import-access fund interoperable with trade-linked purpose-bound transfers. Two export channels are distinguished: physical power exports to neighboring systems or Europe, and electricity-embodied exports of compute services from African data centers. A spatial multi-technology planning model jointly chooses solar photovoltaics, onshore and offshore wind, geothermal, hydropower, concentrating solar power, bioenergy, marine power, storage, transmission, cooling capacity, and compute placement under stochastic resource, financing, land, reliability, and domestic-electrification constraints. A bargaining and politicaleconomy layer identifies when export rents reach citizens rather than foreign sponsors or local elites. We compile descriptive, source-attributed 2025 installed renewable-capacity observations for 54 African sovereign states; examine a restricted cross-section of electricity-access deficits; and construct transparent, explicitly hypothetical country expansion portfolios and time-resolved dispatch experiments. These exercises are engineering counterfactuals, not causal estimates, observed investment projects, or surveyed national resource potential. The argument is conditional rather than categorical: energy exports can relax an external purchasing-power constraint without requiring prior economy-wide industrialization, but neither land abundance nor zero-fuel-cost generation guarantees competitiveness. Welfare gains require secure land rights, affordable finance, local energy-access floors, dependable fiber and transmission, credible export demand, and enforceable mechanisms that convert resource rents into diversified consumption rights and domestic capabilities.
keywords: development economics; renewable energy; AI data centers; infrastructure trade; electricity exports; computable services; land economics; foreign-exchange constraints; purposebound money; Trade-PoC; international access; optimal control; stochastic programming; energy justice

title: Life Beyond Monetary Scarcity
subtitle: Purpose-Bound Money, Human Freedom, and the Transformation of Everyday Life
abstract: What would change in human life if access to essential goods and services no longer depended as extensively on the capacity to acquire unrestricted money? This essay considers a possible future in which purpose-bound monetary instruments, understood as enforceable but restricted claims on specified services, become an ordinary feature of social institutions. Its question is philosophical rather than narrowly monetary. The proposed transformation concerns the conditions under which people are able to plan, refuse, care, work, associate, and pursue experiences that give their lives significance. Drawing on the purpose-oriented architecture developed in Reframing Global Fiscal Architecture, the essay distinguishes the removal of particular purchasing-power barriers from the abolition of scarcity itself. It develops an account of economic freedom as the secure possession of genuinely usable options, rather than either nominal wealth or the mere enumeration of authorized purchases. It argues that predictable access to care, food, education, legal assistance, and cultural participation could change the temporal structure of agency, the moral character of labor contracts, the distribution of social esteem, and the meaning of aspiration. Yet the same technology could establish an unprecedented architecture of permission: classifications of legitimate need, automated exclusions, behavioral surveillance, and private gatekeeping over publicly supported choices. The normative question is therefore not whether programmable entitlements are technologically possible or economically expansive in the abstract, but whether their institutional design can enlarge human capabilities without making persons dependent on unaccountable judgment. The essay proposes a standard of contestable security: entitlements must be reliable enough to support long-term agency, plural enough to respect reasonable differences in conceptions of the good, and governed so that no public or private actor may arbitrarily determine the permissible shape of a life. Purpose-bound money is consequently treated neither as a substitute for justice nor as its enemy, but as one possible instrument whose value must be judged by the freedoms, relationships, and practices of human flourishing it makes possible.
