title: Market Design for a Federated Purpose-Bound Monetary System
subtitle: Sovereign Participation, Corporate Coalitions, and Credible Settlement
abstract: This paper studies the implementation of a federated system of purpose oriented currencies in which a limited mandate Global Central Bank, participating sovereigns, and competing corporate coalitions jointly organize access to designated goods and services. A purpose restriction is modeled as a constraint on the exercise of an entitlement, not as an exemption from resource scarcity or a substitute for settlement funding. The framework distinguishes beneficiary balances, verified merchant receivables, and the funding commitments that discharge those receivables. It integrates household expenditure substitution, differentiated service competition, supplier screening, investment in delivery capacity, sovereign participation, and contingent loss allocation. Conditional implementation results establish when funded entitlement portfolios can be supported by incentive compatible supply contracts and individually rational participation transfers. Separate results characterize the gains from an expanded choice set, the financing and informational limits of those gains, and the conditions under which withdrawal remains credible without undermining outstanding claims. A network formulation connects sectoral demand to common production inputs, while a stochastic control problem makes issuance depend jointly on available capacity, fiscal backing, and verification quality. The extended analysis develops recursive household choice, a small general equilibrium closure, multiproduct competition, coalition bargaining and investment, sovereign private information and limited commitment, network clearing, constrained dynamic issuance, multitask verification, and congested service assignment. Reproducible numerical exercises characterize changes in binding constraints, sustainable insurance, settlement propagation, and timing dependent feedback stability. The central contribution is an integrated implementability frontier: public and private participation can be mutually reinforcing, but a hybrid system dominates feasible alternatives only when its gains from coordination, innovation, and preference matching exceed its real operating costs, financing distortions, informational rents, and settlement risks.
keywords: purpose oriented currency; market design; sovereign participation; corporate coalitions; programmable payments; fiscal settlement; differentiated products; mechanism design.

title: Market Design for Shared AI Infrastructure
subtitle: Investment Incentives, Allocation, and Competition
abstract: This paper studies when a neutral federation of heterogeneous AI computing assets can improve welfare relative to proprietary infrastructure and existing commercial cloud markets. The proposed institution separates residual ownership, contracted service rights, and operational control, while permitting voluntary asset contributions and a competitive market for implementation expertise. A sequence of linked models examines strategic capacity investment with innovation spillovers, reliability pooling under comparable service standards, constrained network allocation, incentive-compatible bidding, fixed-cost recovery, coalition stability, and governance. The analysis identifies conditions under which cooperation creates additional feasible service and conditions under which market power, incomplete contracts, common failure, or financing requirements absorb those gains. An endogenous adoption model links lower compute and implementation costs to both entry and usage; a dynamic framework studies investment timing and hardware reuse; and an energy-market model characterizes rebound when electricity prices respond to demand. The resulting predictions are deliberately conditional. Federation can reduce duplicated reserves while increasing total investment and electricity use, and efficient dispatch need not imply truthful, self-financing, or stable institutional implementation. Analytical proofs, reproducible hypothetical calculations, and an empirical design with congestion spillovers specify how the proposal can be evaluated. The contribution is a testable architecture for selective infrastructure cooperation that preserves competition over models and applications, rather than a presumption in favor of universal ownership consolidation.
keywords: AI infrastructure; industrial organization; capacity investment; mechanism design; stochastic optimization; coalition formation; incomplete contracts; technology adoption; real options; energy rebound.

title: Mechanism Design for Countering Stagflation
subtitle: Purpose-Constrained Commodity Money and the Reallocation of Cost Shocks
abstract: This paper reinterprets stagflation as a problem of inefficient allocation under input scarcity rather than a conventional aggregate demand–supply trade-off. When essential inputs such as energy are scarce and priced uniformly, decentralized market equilibria fail to allocate inputs efficiently across heterogeneous firms, leading to excessive cost pass-through, output contraction, and welfare loss. A mechanism design framework is developed that introduces purpose-constrained, commoditylinked money (Commodity-PoC), which simultaneously modifies effective input prices and imposes quantity constraints. Unlike conventional policy tools such as subsidies or monetary contraction, the proposed mechanism operates jointly in price and quantity space, enabling targeted reallocation of scarce inputs without generating excess demand. The analysis shows that the decentralized equilibrium is inefficient due to input misallocation and that no uniform price-based policy can implement the efficient allocation. The Ramseyoptimal allocation is characterized, and it is shown that the proposed mechanism can implement, or approximate, this allocation under realistic informational and institutional constraints. A calibrated quantitative model demonstrates that the mechanism substantially reduces inflation and output losses following commodity price shocks, generating significant welfare gains relative to both the decentralized equilibrium and standard policy responses. Extensions to an open economy environment indicate that the allocation problem is inherently global, providing a foundation for a coordinating institution analogous to a Global Central Bank. Dynamic extensions show that the mechanism preserves long-run investment incentives under conditional design and remains welfare-improving even in the presence of lobbying and imperfect enforcement. These results suggest that stagflation is not fundamentally a policy trade-off problem, but an implementation problem, and that appropriately designed allocation mechanisms can reconcile price stability and output efficiency under input scarcity.

title: Mechanisms of Inequality
subtitle: A Mathematical Architecture for Structural Containment
abstract: Economic inequality has proven stubbornly resistant to institutional remedies. This paper argues that its persistence reflects not institutional failure alone but the mathematical structure of capital accumulation — the power-law dynamics of multiplicative returns, the Matthew Effect of compounding cross-domain advantage, and Piketty's 𝑟> 𝑔. These are mathematical attractors that institutional reform can slow but cannot redirect. If inequality is mathematical in its genesis, its containment must be mathematical in its design. We propose the Purpose-Bounded Currency System: a multi-domain economic architecture in which distinct exchange units serve distinct domains of human necessity and desire, crossdomain capital mobility is structurally severed, and constitutional inequality constraints are embedded directly in algorithmic governance across seven domains — nutrition, health, housing, education, legal services, mobility, and luxury. Three theorems establish the system's core properties: an unconditional Gini upper bound 𝐺∗= (𝑁0 −1)/(𝑁0 + 1) holding regardless of measurement error or governance failure; complete power-law tail truncation; and a welfare-maximizing trade-off frontier between incentive strength and distributional equality. A two-domain general equilibrium model confirms existence and uniqueness of equilibrium and Pareto superiority for below-floor households. A game-theoretic analysis demonstrates that participation is a dominant strategy for major economies when the fiscal dividend from constitutional floor provision exceeds net transition costs — a condition satisfied for the United States, China, the European Union, and India under empirically calibrated parameters. The system's distributional achievements are architectural rather than operational: they follow from mathematical structure rather than governance execution, making them robust to the measurement error, manipulation, and political capture that have historically eroded redistributive institutions. The mathematical forces generating inequality cannot be stopped. But within a sufficiently well-designed architecture, they cannot destroy what is most fundamental to human dignity.

title: Optimal Price Stabilization with Purpose-Bound Money
subtitle: Endogenous Supply, State-Contingent Conversion Rates, and Protection of Real Purchasing Power
abstract: This paper investigates whether a restricted purchasing claim, combined with credible prospective demand commitments and a transparent, bounded conversion-rate rule, can stabilize sectoral prices without sacrificing the productive investments and service access that the claim was designed to support. A Global Central Bank (GCB) announces eligible demand in advance, accredited suppliers choose capacity, recipients later spend purpose-bound money (PoC), and a prospective conversion factor determines the ordinary-currency purchasing and settlement value of claims under specified contracts. The new objective is explicitly intertemporal: temporary inflation may be socially tolerable when it accompanies capacity expansion and rising household real disposable income, while persistent price pressure, unanchored expectations, and distributional deterioration receive increasing penalties. The planner jointly considers prospective issuance, conversion corridors, claims vintages, minimum essential access, provider participation and fiscal settlement. The analysis also specifies its compatibility boundary with two independent policies. Routine productivity-backed PoC substitution may free treasury cash for sovereign bond retirement, but conversion changes must be reflected in verified net fiscal savings. Exceptional global sovereign debt resets concern conventional monetary liabilities and cannot be stabilized merely by adjusting PoC purchasing power. Existing historical regressions, transfer experiments and hypothetical numerical comparisons are explicitly distinguished from causal evidence of an unobserved global PoC institution. A dynamic supply and price-setting framework yields conditions under which flexible conversion is superior to fixed conversion, as well as precise counterexamples in which rationing, supplier exit, price spillovers or macroeconomic shocks defeat the rule.
keywords: purpose-bound money; programmable purchasing power; forward demand commitments; sectoral inflation; endogenous investment; dynamic monetary control; conversion rates; supply constraints; payment settlement; welfare; field experiments; sectoral market design.

title: Participation, Competition, and Commitment in Purpose-Bound Finance
subtitle: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Sovereign Coordination and Corporate Coalitions
abstract: This paper develops a game-theoretic theory of purpose-bound finance in which sovereign governments, a proposed Global Central Bank (GCB), competing corporate coalitions, independent suppliers, and households interact through sequential participation, financing, procurement, service, and settlement decisions. The central institutional object is a restricted purchasing entitlement coupled to an enforceable, separately funded supplier claim; it is not a legal-tender assumption or an exemption from real scarcity. We distinguish the equilibrium of continuation markets from the stability of national membership and corporate coalitions, and establish when a multi-layer arrangement is supported by individually rational strategies, credible commitments, and solvent balance sheets. A sovereign networkparticipation game exhibits a critical mass and both low- and high-adoption equilibria. A transferable-utility corporate game yields explicit necessary and sufficient conditions for sustaining a proposed coalition against unilateral exit and blocking subcoalitions. Differentiated-product competition shows why consumer voluntariness may be genuine without guaranteeing efficient market power, and why an expanded menu need not raise ex post welfare after endogenous prices and funding change. A dynamic investment game separates credible procurement from merely announced purchasing balances; incentive contracts and verification are subject to principal-agent constraints. We then embed emergency activation, sovereign limited commitment, information design, correlated settlement risk, and a closed real-resource system in a state-contingent institutional game. Conditional results characterize self-enforcing cooperation, fundable service commitments, and the boundary at which common protocols or direct supranational intervention dominate feasible national and private alternatives. A suite of transparently synthetic, executable calculations illustrates multiple equilibria, coalition-core feasibility, platform price competition, supplier investment, repeated-game incentives, reserve requirements, and general-equilibrium crowding out. Neither these calculations nor the institutional design constitute empirical estimates or a claim of demonstrated global implementability. The principal contribution is a unified, falsifiable analytical framework that separates the existence of a beneficial arrangement from the strategic incentives to create, finance, maintain, and use it.
keywords: purpose-bound money; game theory; sovereign participation; global public goods; coalition formation; two-sided platforms; mechanism design; dynamic games; contestable consumer choice; credible settlement; institutional stability; monetary governance.

title: Productivity-Linked Purpose-Bound Money and Sovereign Debt Sustainability
subtitle: Fiscal Substitution, Verified Debt Retirement, and Consistency with Price Stabilization
abstract: This paper examines whether productivity- and capacity-conditioned purpose-bound monetary claims (PoC) can displace verifiable portions of conventional public expenditure, freeing domestic-currency fiscal resources for sovereign debt retirement without presuming costless money creation. The Global Central Bank (GCB) authorizes sector-restricted claims only against audited procurement, supplier participation, credible forward demand, and enforceable treasury debt-retirement covenants. A comprehensive public-sector ledger distinguishes true expenditure displacement from nominal issuance, merchant settlement, tax offsets, reserve remuneration, and subsequent inflation-stabilization costs. This revised analysis makes an explicit institutional boundary with two independent companion policies: a sectoral PoC-toordinary-currency conversion rule, which may alter the real value and settlement cost of a claim, and a treaty-based, exceptional sovereign debt reset, which replaces some creditor claims with conventional monetary liabilities under separate authorization and accounting. The model treats the conversion-rate path as an admissible contingent policy regime and the possibility of a reset as a state-dependent external event rather than assuming either instrument provides fiscal resources automatically. New non-double-counting identities and a counterfactual evaluation matrix prevent the same fiscal saving, creditor redemption, or issuance authorization from being attributed to two programs. The numerical country panel and simulated outcomes remain, respectively, descriptive and assumption-driven: they do not identify the causal effects of a global PoC institution. The central contribution is a falsifiable framework for sovereign debt relief that is valid only when verified ordinary-currency savings exceed the economic value of new public obligations while service access, productive capacity, and medium-term price stability remain protected.
keywords: sovereign debt sustainability; public finance; purpose-bound money; productivity; fiscal substitution; global central bank; interest burden; monetary settlement; dynamic optimal control; policy counterfactuals; fiscal dominance.

title: Programmable Liquidity and Recursive Welfare Stabilization
subtitle: Toward a Computational Theory of Monetary Coordination
abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for purpose-bound monetary systems in which liquidity is no longer treated as fully fungible, but instead operates through constitutionally differentiated and recursively programmable domains of economic coordination. The central argument of the paper is that persistent inequality and recursive welfare instability emerge not solely from ex post distributive failures, but from the structural dynamics of unrestricted fungible liquidity itself. Under conventional monetary architectures, capability-preserving expenditures such as healthcare, education, nutrition, and long-term developmental investment remain continuously vulnerable to speculative displacement, congestion amplification, and recursive concentration dynamics. As a consequence, economic inequality evolves not merely as a static distributional phenomenon, but as a self-reinforcing stochastic process of capability divergence. To address this problem, the paper introduces a recursive segmented monetary framework in which liquidity possesses domain-specific admissibility conditions, adaptive routing constraints, and constitutionally bounded convertibility structures. The proposed system integrates recursive mechanism design, stochastic control theory, segmented general equilibrium analysis, network congestion dynamics, capability-based welfare theory, and programmable CBDC architecture into a unified institutional model. The economy is represented as a high-dimensional stochastic coordination system in which capability accumulation, liquidity propagation, trust evolution, congestion spillovers, and recursive policy intervention interact continuously over time. The paper derives conditions under which Recursive Segmented General Equilibrium exists and demonstrates that recursive capability dynamics remain bounded under appropriate congestion-control and routing constraints. Spectral stability analysis establishes conditions for stable liquidity propagation across segmented monetary networks, while mean-field convergence results show that large heterogeneous-agent economies admit tractable distributional approximation. Computational simulations further suggest that segmented liquidity systems may reduce recursive inequality amplification, improve welfare resilience under large stochastic shocks, stabilize capability persistence, and generate lower long-run congestion volatility relative to unrestricted fungible monetary systems. Beyond its macroeconomic implications, the paper additionally develops a constitutional theory of programmable monetary governance. Because recursively routable liquidity systems possess unprecedented informational and institutional capacity, the framework incorporates formal constraints governing observability, convertibility rights, emergency intervention, judicial review, and decentralized verification. The paper further analyzes the potential role of artificial intelligence and reinforcement learning in adaptive monetary coordination, while emphasizing the necessity of constitutionally bounded AI governance within recursive policylearning environments. More broadly, the paper argues that future monetary systems may increasingly evolve from passive exchange infrastructures into adaptive coordination architectures designed to stabilize long-run capability continuity rather than merely facilitate unrestricted transactional fungibility. The framework therefore proposes a shift in monetary theory away from homogeneous liquidity equilibrium models and toward recursively governed systems of programmable institutional coordination.

title: Protocol Humanism
subtitle: A New Architecture for Money, Capital, and Human Continuity
abstract: This book examines how foundational human guarantees might be embedded in the protocols of economic coordination. Its institutional vision brings together purpose-oriented monetary arrangements, universal starting capital, intergenerational fairness, and governance of computational systems in an era of artificial intelligence. The argument begins from a tension between dynamic innovation and concentrated control over the economic rules through which people participate in markets. This editorial overview is based on the book’s preface; the full text is available in the PDF.

title: Purpose-Bound Finance for Global Crises
subtitle: Direct Supranational Intervention, Sovereign Participation, and State-Contingent Monetary Architecture
abstract: This paper develops a theory of purpose-bound finance for risks that cross borders, propagate through production networks, and overwhelm nationally segmented fiscal mechanisms. Its institutional object is a proposed Global Central Bank (GCB), ordinarily responsible for a shared issuance, verification, and settlement protocol within which sovereign governments retain policy discretion. During a qualifying international emergency, however, the same institution may activate a treaty-limited direct intervention mode: it becomes the contracting principal for contingent service capacity, the issuer of separately funded emergency purchasing entitlements, the allocator of cross-border procurement, and the accountable obligor for certified supplier claims. The transition is not a suspension of scarcity, national law, or fiscal accountability. We distinguish nonconvertible beneficiary rights from merchant receivables and the liquid resources needed to discharge them. A general dynamic model combines heterogeneous sovereigns, endogenous supplier entry and preparedness, private information, correlated catastrophes, monetary and real-resource constraints, and an imperfect crisis signal. Three applications develop distinct mechanisms: a multicountry epidemic with infection externalities and treatment capacity; natural disasters that simultaneously destroy production and transport networks; and persistent climate risk with international mitigation spillovers and locally appropriable adaptation. Conditional propositions characterize the optimal emergency trigger, benefits of pooled reserves, supply-first investment thresholds, sovereign participation, and robust settlement constraints. Artificial intelligence enters as a costly information technology whose predictive and assignment value must be evaluated against conventional rules, strategic data manipulation, and safety constraints. Synthetic calculations illustrate both welfare improvements and reversals as correlation, institutional delay, and fiscal costs vary. The framework does not claim that programmable balances create real resources or that a new global institution is invariably superior to existing contingency finance, competitive procurement, or ordinary vouchers. Its contribution is to characterize when treaty-bounded supranational intervention can coordinate verifiable real services more effectively than decentralized arrangements at an equal full economic cost.
keywords: purpose-bound money; supranational fiscal institutions; crisis finance; epidemic externalities; catastrophic risk; climate finance; state-contingent contracts; coalition formation; emergency procurement; artificial intelligence; settlement solvency; political economy.

title: Recursive Coordination Capitalism
subtitle: Programmable Demand Architectures and Innovation Governance in AI-Scale Economies
abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding purpose-bound money (PBM) as a programmable coordination architecture for AI-scale economies. Unlike conventional monetary systems, which primarily function as generalized exchange and stabilization mechanisms, PBM systems can structure future demand, influence technological diffusion, reduce investment uncertainty, and coordinate long-term innovation dynamics. Building on endogenous growth theory, Schumpeterian creative destruction, capability theory, and computational governance, the paper introduces the concept of Recursive Coordination Capitalism: an emerging economic regime in which technological progress, human capability formation, corporate investment, and institutional adaptation become recursively aligned through programmable demand architectures. The analysis argues that AI-scale economies intensify coordination problems involving innovation timing, labor transition, adoption velocity, and market concentration. In this context, programmable monetary systems may function as adaptive coordination infrastructures capable of accelerating frontier-technology diffusion, stabilizing long-horizon investment, and partially governing technological transition dynamics. At the same time, the paper emphasizes the institutional risks of programmable economic systems, including surveillance expansion, algorithmic governance failure, and excessive centralization. It therefore proposes constitutional computational governance principles centered on democratic oversight, privacy-preserving computation, transparency, decentralization, reversibility, and institutional contestability. The paper concludes that purpose-bound money is not merely a welfare tool, digital currency, or industrial policy instrument, but a programmable coordination infrastructure capable of recursively aligning technological innovation, corporate growth, and human flourishing in increasingly complex AI-scale economies.

title: Reframing Global Fiscal Architecture
subtitle: A Purpose-Oriented System for Money, Welfare, and Labor
abstract: This paper proposes a comprehensive redesign of global public finance through the construction of a programmable and supranational fiscal architecture. The framework centers on five institutional innovations: Purpose-Oriented Currencies (PoCs), Purpose- Bound Accounts (PBAs), Luxury-Purpose Currencies (LPCs), Capital-at-Birth mechanisms, and Embassies of Welfare (EoWs). Together, these instruments enable the issuance, allocation, and governance of digital value based on verified social purpose rather than monetary convertibility or discretionary fiscal transfers. Governed by a proposed Global Central Bank (GCB), the architecture decouples the provision of public goods from territorial taxation and aligns resource flows with measurable human outcomes. The proposed system offers a modular response to persistent structural failures in existing welfare, monetary, and international aid regimes. It integrates purpose-linked monetary issuance, life-cycle capital formation, and transnational service delivery into a coherent institutional design. In addition to its core fiscal mechanisms, the framework explores how externalizing income and asset security from employment reshapes labor incentives and innovation dynamics, extending the architecture beyond redistribution toward systemic reorganization. The paper provides a normative justification, institutional roadmap, and formal economic modeling to support the feasibility of purpose-bound issuance at global scale. By reconceptualizing fiscal sovereignty as programmable, functional, and outcomeoriented, the proposed architecture reframes legitimacy in public finance away from territorial exclusivity toward performance and accountability. This research contributes to debates in institutional economics, monetary design, and global redistribution by offering a blueprint for transnational welfare that combines normative coherence with allocative precision.

title: Reorganizing the National Economy
subtitle: Firms, Networks, and Collective Innovation
abstract: This paper develops a general theory of the National Industrial Federation (NIF): an institutional architecture that preserves private ownership, firm-level managerial autonomy, entry, exit, and product-market competition while coordinating selected complementary resources at the level of an industrial ecosystem. The motivating problem is not that all decentralization is inefficient. Rival experimentation and dispersed information are fundamental sources of discovery. Rather, when research facilities are indivisible, knowledge spillovers cannot be fully appropriated, specialized workers face search frictions, and supplychain investments exhibit complementarities, the individually rational organization of firms can leave socially valuable connections unrealized. Conversely, centralized industrial planning concentrates informational and political risk. The NIF is proposed as a third organizational arrangement: decentralized decisions connected through contestable, transparent, and limitedpurpose common institutions. Its main instruments are voluntary or rule-governed access to shared research infrastructure, interoperable training and credentials, industry-wide labor matching, jointly financed precompetitive innovation, publicly auditable innovation portfolios, and safeguards for market contestability. The paper builds a multi-layer general-equilibrium framework with heterogeneous firms and workers, network spillovers, endogenous participation, congestible collective facilities, public finance, and innovation under uncertainty. It derives conditions under which federation is welfare improving, shows why excessive concentration or an overbroad federation can reverse the result, and proposes empirically falsifiable predictions. A detailed research protocol combines staggered-adoption causal inference, network exposure mappings, quasi-experiments, randomized access lotteries, firmworker linked panels, patent citations, and structural counterfactuals. Cross-country institutions are discussed as partial comparators, not as evidence that the proposed comprehensive model already exists. No original causal estimate is claimed; the quantitative illustrations are hypothetical and are explicitly separated from observed evidence. The paper argues that the appropriate unit of industrial policy may sometimes be the network of complementary firms, rather than the subsidized firm or the state-owned champion, subject to strict competition, fiscal, and democratic-accountability constraints.
keywords: industrial organization; national industrial federation; innovation networks; industrial policy; labor mobility; research spillovers; shared infrastructure; market design; productivity; institutional economics.

title: Reprogramming Capitalism
subtitle: Purpose-Bound Money, Computational Governance, and the Future of Political Economy
abstract: This study develops a theoretical framework for layered monetary systems operating through Purpose-Bound Currency (PoC) architectures. It argues that generalized fungible money, while historically effective for industrial-era coordination, structurally transmits financial instability, speculative volatility, and inflationary pressures into capability-generating sectors such as healthcare, education, housing, and nutrition. The paper proposes a differentiated monetary architecture in which selected domains of socially foundational consumption operate through purpose-bound monetary layers partially insulated from speculative financial circulation. By embedding institutional constraints directly into monetary circulation, PoC systems potentially stabilize capability formation while attenuating inflationary and financial-instability transmission mechanisms. Integrating macroeconomics, monetary theory, financial instability theory, capability theory, computational governance, and systems analysis, the study develops dynamic models of segmented monetary circulation, cybernetic stabilization, programmable credit allocation, institutional learning, and computational coordination. It further argues that advances in computation, artificial intelligence, and real-time informational systems fundamentally expand the feasible frontier of institutional coordination beyond the generalized monetary architectures of industrial capitalism. The paper concludes that programmable monetary systems may represent not merely a monetary innovation, but part of a broader transition from industrial market civilization toward computationally coordinated political-economic systems centered on capability stabilization, adaptive governance, and differentiated institutional coordination.

title: Rethinking Microfinance
subtitle: Purpose-Bound Money, Microenterprise Development, and Social Welfare
abstract: The economic case for microenterprise development is commonly judged by producer earnings, enterprise survival, productivity, and the extent to which small firms eventually scale into larger productive organizations. These are indispensable criteria, but they are not exhaustive measures of economic welfare. Entry by neighborhood firms can modify the choice set, local price dispersion, service convenience, quality differentiation, opening hours, spatial accessibility, and the allocation of expenditure across households with different income and mobility constraints. The claim that subsistence entrepreneurship cannot substitute for industrial transformation is therefore logically consistent with a separate claim that carefully selected small-firm entry can raise consumer welfare even when measured aggregate productivity changes little. This study formalizes that distinction and examines a policy instrument, Startup Purpose-Bound Money (Startup-PoC), that would reimburse an independently verified fraction of eligible startup investment through non-transferable, time-limited, auditable purchasing claims. Startup-PoC is distinguished from an unrestricted grant, a loan, and an unconditional increase in the money stock. The paper develops a differentiatedproducts model with heterogeneous households, endogenous entry and exit, spatial search costs, supplier capacity, endogenous capital formation, and fiscal-monetary settlement. It derives conditions under which entry subsidies increase or decrease total welfare, characterizes interactions with separately funded consumer-side transfers, and states fiscal and inflation constraints that prevent the treatment of restricted claims as costless resources. A prospective cluster-randomized factorial design and a transparent synthetic 400-market stress test show how to investigate entry, distribution, variety, and fiscal opportunity costs without mislabeling counterfactual calculations as causal evidence. The central proposition is conditional rather than universal: microenterprise entry may generate substantial consumer-side gains, but these gains justify public support only when they exceed business stealing, duplicated setup costs, congestion, administrative leakage, and the shadow cost of public finance.
keywords: purpose-bound money; entrepreneurship; microenterprise; consumer surplus; firm entry; differentiated products; development economics; local markets; monetary financing; fiscal incidence; program evaluation; general equilibrium.

title: Scaling Solidarity
subtitle: Programmable Money and the Economics of Global Welfare Networks
abstract: Purpose-bound purchasing power can connect households, service providers, investors, and governments through a common institutional infrastructure. Whether that infrastructure generates a socially valuable network, however, depends on more than the number of wallets or the precision of expenditure restrictions. This paper develops a theory of a federated welfare platform combining purpose-oriented currencies, Capital at Birth, and Embassies of Welfare. The central mechanism is a complementarity between effective household participation and credible, geographically accessible supply. A baseline participation model identifies the conditions for a unique equilibrium, local amplification, and coordination failure. Extensions incorporate capacity investment, endogenous quality, household cash displacement, redemption risk, spatial access, information incentives, international participation, and intergenerational asset ownership. We derive conditions under which restrictions can improve a second-best allocation, show why global participation does not establish fiscal neutrality, and distinguish financial diversification from the elimination of aggregate risk. A production-network formulation characterizes price spillovers outside eligible sectors; a robust issuance rule links commitments to conservative estimates of deliverable capacity and backing. Explicit counterexamples demonstrate that participation, measured transactions, and provider revenue can rise while welfare falls. The institutional implication is a conditional sequencing principle: establish backing, settlement credibility, contestable supply, and effective access before scaling entitlements. Numerical exercises illustrate the model rather than estimate policy effects. The paper concludes with a staged empirical design that distinguishes purchasing-power effects from administrative simplification, provider investment, and genuine network complementarities.
keywords: purpose-bound money; multisided platforms; welfare provision; network effects; market design; international cooperation; capital endowments; public finance.

title: Supply Before Spending
subtitle: Industrial Capacity, Entrepreneurial Entry, and Demand Commitments in a Purpose-Bound Economy
abstract: This paper develops a theory of supply-first demand commitments: an institutional arrangement in which future purchasing power is credibly specified before it is spent, private productive capacity is built and verified before large-scale redemption occurs, and market access is subsequently activated in accordance with measured supply conditions. The mechanism is designed for a purpose-bound monetary system (PoC), in which transfers are restricted to specified goods or services, subject to eligibility, expiry, and audit rules, and ordinarily cannot be converted into unrestricted currency. The central innovation is not the proposition that productive capacity is desirable before expenditure. It is the design of an intertemporal coordination mechanism that joins credible demand commitments, endogenous scale investment by incumbent firms, venture entry and experimentation, complementarity across upstream and downstream industries, capacity-contingent transfer activation, and a consolidated public balance-sheet constraint. A dynamic heterogeneous-firm model nests fixed costs, endogenous product variety, financial frictions, quality investment, input-output dependencies, imperfect information about future demand, and an occasionally binding capacity constraint. We characterize the investment and entry margins, conditions under which commitments can select a higher-capacity equilibrium, and circumstances in which delayed activation reduces the price response to transfers. The principal propositions are conditional: investment requires commitment credibility; rivalry can erode inefficient markups only if contracting avoids foreclosure; supply investment itself can produce transitional inflation; and an erroneous forecast or an overly generous guarantee may generate overcapacity, fiscal losses, and concentration. A complementary empirical program specifies contract-level data construction, staggered-adoption difference-in-differences, event-study identification, regression discontinuity, randomized phase-in, structural estimation, and transparent counterfactual simulation. Existing evidence on advance market commitments and industrial policy motivates the framework but does not constitute causal proof that a PoC system would outperform unrestricted transfers. The paper concludes with an implementable policy architecture and explicitly testable rejection criteria.
keywords: purpose-bound money; supply-first sequencing; advance market commitments; industrial organization; endogenous entry; capacity investment; market design; industrial policy; contingent activation; inflation; welfare.

title: The Computational Organization of Innovation
subtitle: Capital Allocation, Platform Power, and Technological Governance in AI-Scale Economies
abstract: This paper develops a Schumpeterian framework for innovation governance under AI-scale economies characterized by extreme technological scale, increasing returns to innovation, and growing concentration of computational and financial power. Building upon the concept of creative destruction, the paper argues that traditional industrial-era capital allocation mechanisms become increasingly insufficient as frontier technological systems require hyperscale compute infrastructure, large fixed costs, and platform-centered innovation ecosystems. To address this problem, the paper introduces Purpose-Bound Innovation Capital (PBIC): a programmable monetary and financial architecture designed to direct innovation financing toward scientifically and technologically productive activities rather than unrestricted speculative circulation. The framework formalizes how computational governance systems can recycle monopoly rents into future innovation capacity, mitigate excessive platform concentration, and sustain long-run innovative dynamism under AI-scale technological conditions. The paper further develops recursive models of innovation concentration, monopoly-rent recycling, computational coordination, and transition dynamics while proposing institutional mechanisms for global innovation governance in the age of artificial intelligence. Rather than rejecting capitalism or innovation-driven competition, the paper develops a framework for preserving Schumpeterian creative destruction under conditions where advanced technological economies increasingly exceed the coordination capacity of traditional industrial institutions.

title: The Economics of Aesthetic Experience
subtitle: Aesthetic Opportunity and the Design of Entitlements, Markets, and Institutions
abstract: Access to aesthetic experience is shaped jointly by income, information, geography, scarce capacity, and the institutions through which consumers and suppliers meet. This paper develops a marketdesign framework for luxury-purpose currency and aesthetic basic income, interpreted as restricted purchasing rights embedded in a competitive system of experience provision. The analysis separates intrinsic enjoyment from positional value, nominal balances from attainable opportunities, and issuer authorization from credible settlement. It establishes a cash-dominance benchmark and then studies departures arising from distributional objectives, external effects, supply commitments, private information, and dynamic preference discovery. A sequence of tractable models characterizes subsidy incidence with universal and targeted eligibility, incentivecompatible procurement, the option value of learning, rollover, capacity choice under uncertain demand, spatial allocation, platform dependence, and correlated redemption risk. The results identify both the potential gains from integrating portable entitlements with verifiable supply and the conditions under which restrictions merely transfer rents or reduce household discretion. Formal propositions, proofs, numerical illustrations, and an evaluation design connect institutional choices to observable outcomes. The paper does not infer welfare from redemption or treat restricted issuance as a source of real resources. Its central conclusion is that experiential access is an implementability problem: a credible entitlement must jointly satisfy household choice, supplier incentives, physical feasibility, and fiscal coverage, and must outperform feasible alternatives under an explicit welfare criterion.
keywords: experiential welfare; aesthetic opportunity; in-kind transfers; market design; incentive compatibility; cultural participation; platform competition; fiscal risk.

title: The Informational Transformation of Capitalism
subtitle: From Price Discovery to Purpose Discovery
abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical framework for redesigning capital markets under conditions of increasingly recursive informational capitalism. It argues that advanced capitalism is transitioning from primarily price-mediated market coordination toward adaptive recursive coordination systems integrating informational infrastructures, AI-mediated governance, legitimacy dynamics, and purpose-oriented capital allocation mechanisms. Within this transformation, conventional capital markets increasingly encounter structural limitations in coordinating long-term innovation, social stability, and adaptive economic development. To address these limitations, the paper introduces the concept of purpose-oriented capital markets as institutional architectures capable of directing capital allocation toward recursively coordinated developmental objectives. The analysis develops a framework in which capital markets evolve from speculative exchange systems into adaptive coordination infrastructures integrating programmable incentives, innovation-oriented allocation mechanisms, recursive governance systems, and purpose-bound investment structures. The paper further develops formal models of recursive coordination, adaptive governance, legitimacy stabilization, and bounded institutional recursion while analyzing systemic risks associated with recursive capitalism, including governance concentration, informational monopolization, synchronization instability, and recursive amplification dynamics. In response, the paper argues that long-run systemic resilience increasingly depends upon distributed governance, institutional modularity, recursive transparency, and bounded recursive coordination. More broadly, the paper argues that recursive capitalism represents not merely technological modernization or financial innovation, but a transformation in the architecture of politicaleconomic coordination itself. The central challenge of future political economy therefore increasingly becomes not only how markets allocate resources, but how recursively adaptive societies stabilize recursive coordination under conditions of accelerating informational complexity.

title: A New Architecture for Financial Stability
subtitle: Countercyclical Collateral and Cash-Flow Insurance
abstract: Financial crises are often amplified by the interaction of deteriorating collateral values, impaired operating cash flows, creditor withdrawals, and forced asset sales. Existing macroprudential arrangements primarily fortify intermediaries’ balance sheets, while private liquidity management and social-insurance arrangements address different dimensions of income risk. This paper develops a unified architecture of countercyclical collateral and cash-flow insurance intended to protect viable economic activity without guaranteeing pre-crisis asset prices or socializing every private loss. During expansions, contributions related to realized credit growth, risk-sensitive asset transactions, and discretionary cash-flow surpluses accumulate in distinct, legally segregated funds. During contractions, a collateral facility offers capped, partially priced guarantees against covenant-driven deleveraging, while a cash-flow facility provides temporary, targeted liquidity assistance. A contingent and budget-limited fiscal backstop operates only after predefined exhaustion and systemic-risk tests. A dynamic heterogeneous-agent framework connects collateral constraints, rollover frictions, endogenous fire-sale prices, buffer accumulation, borrower selection, bank capital, and public contingent liabilities. The paper derives local equilibrium conditions, establishes when intervention attenuates liquidation amplification, shows why strict instrument complementarity requires specific production or survival nonconvexities, and formalizes solvency, moral-hazard, and sovereign-risk constraints. A reproducible stylized stress test illustrates possible channels but does not constitute empirical evidence. The empirical agenda combines loan-level credit registers, corporate accounts, granular collateral valuations, and policy-threshold variation in difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables, and dynamic panel designs. A fully specified governance protocol addresses valuation, trigger rules, contribution schedules, risk sharing, asset encumbrance, fiscal ceilings, claims administration, and resolution. The principal contribution is an integrated, testable policy architecture rather than a claim to invent countercyclical provisioning, precautionary saving, or asset-price insurance individually.
keywords: financial stability; collateral constraints; cash-flow insurance; countercyclical buffers; macroprudential policy; fire sales; public guarantees; optimal fiscal insurance; systemic risk

title: Beyond Interest Rates
subtitle: A New Architecture for Macroeconomic Policy
abstract: Macroeconomic policy confronts a problem of assignment: an instrument that influences several outcomes at once cannot generally deliver independently specified objectives. A policy rate that restrains spending also changes debt service, credit supply, asset valuations, exchange rates, and employment. Existing fiscal, prudential, and external-sector instruments already provide ways to manage these interactions. This paper asks a more specific question: can a purpose-bound payment instrument extend the feasible set of a well-designed conventional policy mix, rather than merely replicate a targeted fiscal program in a different technological form? The paper distinguishes instrument effectiveness from instrument labels, derives a local criterion for incremental stabilization value, and develops an accounting and institutional framework in which restricted payments are financed explicitly and evaluated against comparable vouchers and transfers. A household cash-flow model, a constrained investment model, and a small-open-economy extension identify channels through which interest-rate changes and international financial disturbances can impair essential access and productive activity. A dynamic quadratic policy model characterizes the limits of interest-rate stabilization, the role of additional instruments, and the consequences of binding budgets and imperfect implementation. Numerical experiments compare three nested policy menus under common resource constraints. In the illustrative environment, conventional instruments account for most of the achievable improvement; the marginal benefit of purpose-bound payments is conditional and sometimes insufficient to justify their additional cost. Historical U.S. quarterly data provide a descriptive examination of heterogeneous interest-rate associations, while published quasi-experimental and international evidence motivates a prospective identification strategy. The paper does not claim that monetary design abolishes the open-economy trilemma or permits costless public expenditure. Its contribution is a framework for determining when additional, functionally differentiated instruments are economically distinct, institutionally feasible, and useful for macroeconomic stabilization.
keywords: policy assignment; monetary transmission; purpose-bound payments; fiscal-monetary coordination; macroprudential policy; financial accelerator; external shocks; policy autonomy

title: Breaking the Cycle of Inequality
subtitle: A Theory of Cross-Domain Economic Transmission
abstract: This paper develops a theory of inequality as a dynamic system of mutually reinforcing economic disadvantages rather than as a scalar distribution of income or wealth. Financial resources influence access to housing, health care, education and other inputs into human capability; the resulting disparities influence earnings, savings and the resources available to the next generation. The relevant object for policy is therefore not merely the magnitude of each gap but the structure of transmission among them. A multidimensional state-space model distinguishes persistent inequality within a domain from the propagation of disadvantage across domains. Under a nonnegative linear approximation, the spectral radius characterizes asymptotic amplification, while a resolvent measures the cumulative consequences of a transitory shock. A separate analysis of heterogeneous households, constrained service markets and intergenerational transitions clarifies when these aggregate representations are defensible. The framework derives conditions under which interventions targeting transmission edges dominate policies addressing only current gaps, while allowing cash transfers, public provision and purpose-bound purchasing rights to outperform one another under different constraints. A descriptive analysis of published PISA 2022 statistics and a synthesis of causal evidence from housing, health insurance, nutrition, schooling and cash-transfer reforms establish empirical motivation; they do not identify the full transmission matrix. Reproducible numerical experiments quantify dynamic amplification, sensitivity to institutional leakage and the consequences of policy allocation under explicitly hypothetical parameters. The paper provides a feasible identification and replication protocol for estimating the structural model with longitudinal data. The central implication is that an economy can preserve meaningful differences in financial rewards while reducing the extent to which those differences determine access to essential capabilities. This proposition is conditional on resource feasibility, institutional quality and credible evidence rather than on a presumed superiority of any particular monetary architecture.
keywords: multidimensional inequality; cumulative advantage; economic mobility; human capital; dynamic networks; public economics; policy design; purpose-bound transfers

title: Liquidity Segmentation and Welfare Resilience
subtitle: Dynamic Allocation under Economic Shocks
abstract: This paper studies whether contingent restrictions on the use and conversion of public transfer claims can improve insurance against heterogeneous economic shocks. Rather than presuming that earmarked liquidity is intrinsically superior to fungible money, it treats segmentation as a costly institutional technology whose value depends on externalities, incomplete insurance, supplier capacity, private information, and fiscal settlement. An economy with heterogeneous households, irreversible capability losses, domain-specific providers, a network of legally admissible conversions, and aggregate and idiosyncratic shocks is developed. The analysis establishes an equivalence result for inframarginal restrictions; a welfare condition for binding restrictions; an existence and uniqueness result for a regularized routing problem; an accounting proposition showing why end-user restrictions do not by themselves extinguish fiscal obligations; a stability condition for adaptive feedback; and a constrained-planner characterization with downside-risk penalties. The paper also implements a fully labeled synthetic computational experiment involving four transfer regimes under the same authorized budget. In the benchmark parameterization, adaptive restricted assistance improves average simulated welfare relative to unrestricted transfers, but the ranking reverses under scarce supply. The quantitative exercise is a mechanism test, not a causal evaluation of a real-world policy. Published randomized and administrative evidence is reviewed as external motivation, without treating it as validation of the proposed architecture. The resulting theory identifies a limited but potentially valuable role for purpose-bound liquidity: preventing high-social-cost interruptions when a verifiable critical-use margin is binding, administrative errors are controllable, and provider capacity and fiscal settlement can accommodate the intervention.
keywords: liquidity segmentation; social insurance; automatic stabilizers; stochastic control; purpose-bound transfers; capability persistence; network flows; constrained optimization; welfare economics

title: Monetary Design and Inflation
subtitle: A Structural Theory of Price Stability
abstract: The price consequences of monetary expansion depend on the expenditure opportunities created by issuance and the capacity of the economy to meet the resulting demand. This paper develops a structural framework for purpose-bound currency (PoC), a restricted purchasing instrument that can be redeemed only for specified goods and services. Unlike a universal claim about money neutrality, the analysis distinguishes the legal non-convertibility of an instrument from the economic interdependence of markets. A household model with separate spending constraints, a capacity-constrained supply system, and an explicit settlement mechanism identify conditions under which additional purchasing rights increase access without raising transaction prices. These conditions can fail through displacement of ordinary expenditure, shared inputs, provider market power, redemption into unrestricted money, or limited supply. A multisector comparative-static system characterizes direct and indirect price responses; a dynamic issuance problem incorporates investment delays, stochastic capacity, model uncertainty, and price safeguards. Reproducible numerical experiments compare restricted and unrestricted transfers at equal nominal allocations and examine the trade-off between access and price stability. Evidence from randomized cash-versus-in-kind transfers and retail studies of food benefits supports the relevance of supply and spending composition, while remaining insufficient to identify the causal effect of the proposed monetary architecture. A descriptive analysis of observed US manufacturing utilization and producer prices from 2000 to 2025 highlights the limits of aggregate slack measures. A pilot-based empirical design specifies the data and variation necessary for causal identification. The contribution is a conditional theory of monetary design, not a claim that monetary quantities or macroeconomic constraints cease to matter.
keywords: purpose-bound currency; inflation; sectoral capacity; monetary transmission; restricted transfers; market design; welfare; stochastic control

title: Optimal Inequality
subtitle: A Mathematical Theory of Distribution, Incentives, and Social Welfare
abstract: This paper develops a framework for evaluating inequality as a design constraint on economic allocation rather than as a single observed statistic to be minimized. The central distinction is between a mathematical guarantee on the dispersion of a specified allocation, the distribution actually generated by an incentive-compatible mechanism, and the distribution a social planner would prefer after accounting for resource costs, heterogeneity, and behavioral responses. A sharp population Gini bound is derived for positive allocations with a finite maximum-to-minimum ratio, together with fixed-mean refinements, top-share bounds, and related results for generalized entropy and the Atkinson index. A multidomain extension shows how protected service entitlements and unequal discretionary rewards can coexist, but also identifies conditions under which a monetary entitlement fails to secure a real service outcome. The paper embeds distributional bounds in a screening problem, a tractable labor-supply economy, an entrepreneurial choice model, and a capacity-constrained public-service economy. In the labor-supply economy, an explicit grid search compares balanced-budget linear redistribution with a capped reward schedule over 27 combinations of productivity dispersion, effort elasticity, and social inequality aversion. Under the specified preferences, a cap offers no detectable welfare improvement over the best linear schedule in this grid; binding ratio constraints instead impose measurable welfare costs. This negative result is informative: an upper bound should not be confused with a universally optimal intervention. Descriptive calculations using World Bank distribution statistics for eleven economies and U.S. Census household income shares illustrate the difference between observed inequality, grouped-data inequality, and hypothetical design guarantees. The paper concludes with a conditional policy framework that distinguishes minimum capabilities, incentive-compatible rewards, economic rents, and control rights. Its numerical experiments are reproducible model calculations, not causal estimates of an implemented cap.
keywords: inequality bounds; optimal redistribution; social welfare; incentive compatibility; distributional constraints; labor supply; public services; economic rents

title: Programmable Demand and Innovation Investment
subtitle: AI Adoption under Uncertainty
abstract: This paper extends the theory of advance market commitments to downstream investment in artificial-intelligence-enabled services. A purchasing promise can reduce the risk of irreversible organizational transformation only when it is enforceable, creditworthy, and conditional on verifiable delivery. The proposed programmable demand commitment is therefore a contract-design instrument, not a claim that blockchain or purpose-bound money independently creates resources. A model of heterogeneous firms combines uncertain service demand, risk aversion, financing constraints, complementary organizational capital, upstream capacity, and endogenous adoption spillovers. It derives the cost of a minimum-demand floor, the conditions for higher investment, an equilibrium uniqueness threshold, and cases in which procurement displaces private uses or increases market power. A transparent synthetic experiment compares demand commitments, integration grants, and hybrids at approximately equal expected expenditure. A Korean-won example translates normalized exposure into auditable quantities without claiming external calibration. Finally, a randomized procurement pilot design specifies outcomes and identification assumptions. Legal enforceability, verification errors, and risk allocation—not the payment technology—govern the intervention’s potential value.
keywords: AI adoption; advance market commitments; public procurement; irreversible investment; demand uncertainty; organizational capital; fiscal risk; technology diffusion

title: Purpose-Bound Transfers, Idle Capacity, and Inflation
subtitle: A Theory of Welfare Provision
abstract: This paper examines whether restricting public transfers to specified essential services can expand effective access without imposing an equivalent increase in sectoral inflation. It rejects the premise that nonfungibility, by itself, relaxes an economy’s real-resource constraint. Instead, the analysis identifies a narrower mechanism: a payment instrument tied to a particular service may alter the timing and composition of demand, the credibility of provider commitments, and the distribution of capacity investment. The economic case for such an arrangement therefore depends jointly on the household’s inframarginal expenditure, provider entry and spare capacity, the costs of fiscal settlement, and the pass-through of provider revenue into unrestricted money. A two-sector general-equilibrium economy is developed with heterogeneous households, capacity-constrained providers, imperfect competition, and a government that faces a consolidated intertemporal budget constraint. A restricted transfer is shown to be locally equivalent to cash whenever its categorical constraint is slack; when the constraint binds, it can increase desired consumption of the eligible good and raise its price. Under specified conditions, however, verifiable supply contracts and utilization-contingent allocation permit greater real service provision per unit of public expenditure. The paper derives thresholds for price containment, capacity expansion, optimal transfer design, provider rents, and household welfare, including counterexamples where restrictions fail. An explicitly illustrative computational experiment compares four fiscally comparable arrangements over stochastic demand shocks. It is supplemented by a critical synthesis of published evidence on food assistance, retail prices, and program administration, and by a preregistration-ready empirical identification agenda. No observational estimate or simulation is represented as a causal evaluation of the proposed institution. The contribution is a falsifiable theory of when supply-linked purpose-bound transfers may outperform, equal, or underperform conventional cash assistance.
keywords: purpose-bound transfers; in-kind provision; idle capacity; inflation; market power; supplier contracting; social insurance; public finance; empirical identification

title: Redesigning Shareholder Capitalism
subtitle: A New Theory of Capital Allocation and Social Value
abstract: The paper develops a conditional theory of purpose-oriented capital allocation within a shareholder-based market economy. Conventional markets aggregate information about expected monetizable returns, but important external consequences of innovation remain outside firm cash flows. We model an auxiliary financing channel that combines commercial returns with independently estimated social contributions under a binding aggregate resource constraint. For a two-project economy, we derive an exact welfare comparison and show that the optimal weight on purpose information declines as measurement error increases. In a multiproject environment, strategic disclosure, audit costs, dynamic innovation spillovers, and correlated evaluation feedback can reverse the gains from purpose-directed investment. The framework separates contractual financial claims from verified social-outcome claims, emphasizing additional real capital formation, budget balance, and the legitimacy of heterogeneous welfare preferences. An observed-data exercise re-estimates standard investment equations using 220 historical firm-year observations from the Grunfeld panel; these data do not identify any purpose-finance effect. A distinct computational experiment simulates 450 economies of 120 projects and illustrates a model-dependent welfare gain of 6.20 percent under accurate signals, falling to a loss of 10.50 percent under severe noise. The central empirical agenda is an independently audited, preregistered experiment isolating information from financial subsidy effects. The proposal is neither a general rejection of shareholder capitalism nor a claim that social value can be reduced to an objective universal score. Its contribution is a set of falsifiable conditions under which social-purpose information may improve, or worsen, decentralized investment and innovation decisions.
keywords: Capital allocation; shareholder welfare; social externalities; directed innovation; sustainable finance; information design; mechanism design; evaluation; institutional economics

title: The Economics of Preference Diversity
subtitle: Democracy, Coordination, and Collective Choice
abstract: This paper develops a political-economic framework for democratic choice under irreducible preference diversity, combining combinatorial social-choice analysis with a strategically founded model of consultation, lobbying, information transmission, agenda control, and electoral accountability. It complements, rather than disputes, Arrow's impossibility theorem. Strict linear orders over n alternatives number n!, while directed circular arrangements modulo rotation number (n−1)!, independent of electorate size; neither count implies that actual pairwise majorities must cycle. Our normative claim is that pluralist democracy need not seek a unique complete public preference ordering as the output of every choice procedure. Its institutional task is to reconcile feasible concurrent policies and govern unavoidable conflicts through legitimate, contestable procedures. We propose regular election of representatives, transparent legislative votes, and recurring, primarily advisory online policy consultation with fiscal and constitutional safeguards. The central theoretical contribution endogenizes participation distortion previously treated as a fixed bias: citizens choose whether to participate, organized groups choose costly mobilization, an informed expert sends strategic cheap-talk messages, and a reelection-sensitive politician chooses agenda access and policy. In a tractable sequential game we characterize a perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish uniqueness of organized mobilization under stated conditions, derive informative two-message communication cutoffs, and obtain an explicit agenda-inclusion threshold. The equilibrium online-public opinion gap arises from the interaction of mobilization technology and electoral incentives; population calibration removes this specific incentive under stringent observability and exclusion assumptions. Analytical counterfactuals, exact preference-profile enumeration, synthetic THE ECONOMICS OF PREFERENCE DIVERSITY • RESEARCH MANUSCRIPT simulations, and an external literature review clarify when additional consultation may improve information and when it may strengthen strategic capture. Empirical identification protocols are provided, but no causal effect of the full proposal is asserted without data. The contribution is an analytically disciplined framework for democratic coordination when disagreement persists and political agents behave strategically.
keywords: Arrow's impossibility theorem; circular permutations; preference diversity; perfect Bayesian equilibrium; cheap talk; lobbying; agenda control; political pandering; continuous policy consultation; procedural legitimacy
